description: We are a group of Computer Science and Data Engineering students from the Poznań University of Life Sciences. We chose this project to try and create a more accessible tool for anyone to try image sonification. The cat is Pitek- he is our spirit animal
summary: JukeBox is a browser-based web application that translates NASA Earth images and user-uploaded pictures into music using image sonification, mapping horizontal position to time, vertical position to pitch, and brightness to loudness. It transforms complex, silent satellite data - such as surface winds, carbon monoxide, and cloud covers - into an interactive audio-visual experience complete with custom backing beats, presets, and WAV/MIDI exports, running entirely client-side using vanilla JavaScript, the Web Audio API, and WebGL2. It bridges the gap between science and art, transforming abstract environmental data, while also giving people who cannot fully experience our planet visually a unique way to feel it through music.
details:
For a more detailed description of the project, check out our repository: https://github.com/Tomson601/Tomson601.github.io

JukeBox is a web application that lets people "listen to our planet" by turning NASA images of Earth, or any other pictures you provide, into music. Our task was to create an interface, script, or application that combines visual frames with dynamic sonification generated in real time. In short, we wanted to give people the chance to literally "hear" the Earth by transforming images into music—while also enabling those who cannot fully experience our planet through sight to perceive it through sound.

The application features a virtual station (jukebox interface) where you can choose a pre-set image album. The system is very intuitive: you can easily stop playback, change and switch individual frames, control sound parameters and presets, and upload your own graphics. Finally, the finished piece can be easily downloaded to your disk in WAV or MIDI format.

We used authentic images of Earth from the NASA EPIC satellite, along with climate and meteorological maps from NASA GMAO and GPM.

First, the image is converted to grayscale and its contrast is stretched. Next, the picture is placed onto a grid where horizontal movement from left to right determines time, meaning every vertical slice is one beat, while vertical position from bottom to top maps to pitch with higher points playing higher notes. Finally, pixel brightness decides loudness where bright elements play louder while dark ones stay silent, and every note is automatically snapped to a chosen musical scale so the result always sounds harmonious and in key. 

Our program has a really great range of features, such as:

  • Record magazine with ready-made albums of NASA climate maps.
  • Live Earth photos fetched from the NASA EPIC satellite.
  • Custom images allowing you to upload and convert your own graphic files.
  • Beat editor and backing beat featuring a 16-step grid and drum styles.
  • Sound presets and advanced settings providing full control over the audio.
  • Exporting songs to WAV or MIDI formats.

Additionally, the website also features an accessibility options tab—parameters such as larger font sizing, reduced motion for elements, and high contrast settings are available.

Although NASA and other institutions have previously created projects related to the sonification of space data, most of them are merely passive, pre-recorded videos where the user cannot change anything. Our JukeBox is different and much more powerful because it is a fully interactive instrument running directly in the browser.

We used JavaScript, the Web Audio API for sound synthesis, Canvas 2D, and WebGL2. As for the data, we used authentic Earth photos from the NASA EPIC satellite as well as climate and meteorological maps from NASA GMAO and GPM.
